anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to touch more data, rows, or time than business logic requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer selects or reuses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan despite having reasonably accurate statistics.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer cannot supply the read/write bandwidth or IOPS demanded, causing sustained device-level saturation.

When all three root causes are active, the database exhibits extreme and erratic latency: the same statements repeatedly surface in slow-query and wait-events logs with swings between moderate and catastrophic response times; buffer cache hit ratios collapse, page read and write latencies spike, and long-running transactions accumulate large lock-hold times. Execution plans may oscillate between inefficient full scans and cached sub-optimal plans, amplifying I/O volume precisely when the storage subsystem is already saturated. Application sessions experience timeouts, deadlock retries, and connection pool exhaustion, while system metrics show moderate CPU, soaring I/O wait, deep device queues, and excessive redo/transaction log flush delays.

Causally, overly broad or chatty SQL (Workload Logic Anomaly) inflates the logical work the optimizer must translate into physical access paths. If the optimizer then selects a poor plan (Query Plan Selection Anomaly)—such as hash or nested-loop joins that read vast table portions or disable partition pruning—the physical I/O demand balloons. This surge in random and sequential reads/writes drives the underlying disks or flash tiers past their throughput limits (Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly). In turn, the elevated I/O latency feeds back to the optimizer’s feedback mechanisms and to application latency thresholds, increasing the likelihood of plan invalidations, parameter-sensitive plan flips, and additional retries that further increase the workload volume. The intertwined effects create a self-reinforcing spiral where bad logic produces bad plans, bad plans overload storage, and storage saturation magnifies every inefficiency, severely degrading overall database performance and stability.

entry.official_description: %d error logging component(s) failed to flush. For file-based logs this can happen when the path or permissions of the log-file have changed. Failure to flush filed-based logs may affect log-rotation.
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with file creation, filesystem access, write durability, log persistence, tablespace management, or storage-capacity boundaries.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect filesystem capacity and permissions, verify persistence paths, review log and data placement, and check whether storage latency or write failures are affecting the engine.
